The weed with a parachute.

Coat buttons (Tridax) has a small daisy-like flower: cream rays around a yellow centre, on a long bare stalk above toothed leaves. Each of its small seeds carries a feathery tuft, so the wind picks them up and carries them off. That is why it is so often one of the first weeds to appear on ground that has just been cleared or dug: bare soil, and nothing there yet to shade it out.

Along a wall, a strip, not a scatter.

Weeds at a boundary wall do not spread across the whole plot: they grow in a narrow line right at the base, where soil and moisture collect against the wall. So that is where the granules go, in a narrow strip along that line and nowhere else, stopping well short of any pot, bed or plant you want to keep.

Sprinkle onto the soil, water lightly, leave it. No spray, no mixing. The granules clear whatever they reach, so never use them on lawns, beds or crops you are keeping. Wear gloves; keep away from children, pets and plants you want.

Before you clear a patch, ask four questions.

1. Is anything here you want to keep? Then work around it by hand or with a rake; granules never go near it.
2. Is it flowering or seeding? Take the heads off first and bag them, so the seed does not drop while you work.
3. Does it spread by runners or tubers, like doob or nutgrass? Pulling snaps them and leaves pieces behind that grow again.
4. Is it a wall base, path or corner you want completely bare? That is where granules belong: sprinkle, water lightly, leave it.

Dig deep to weed, and you plant the next batch.

Every bed holds a bank of weed seeds, buried at all depths. Most of them only sprout from the top few centimetres, where there is light. Dig a spade deep to get the weeds out and you turn buried seeds up to the surface, where they wake up. A shallow stroke through the top layer lifts the weeds that are growing and leaves the buried seeds where they are, waiting in the dark.

That shallow stroke is what our 5-teeth rake head is for. It is a head only: handle not included; fits a standard wooden pole.

The peepal on your wall was planted by a bird.

Birds eat peepal and banyan figs, then sit on parapets, terrace edges, wall tops and wires. The seeds pass through and drop right there, into a joint or crack in the wall. That is why a peepal seedling can appear on a wall with no tree anywhere nearby.

The roots follow the crack into the wall, and as they thicken they can widen it. So pull the seedling out while it is still small, roots and all, instead of cutting off the top.

Dig in. Pull back. Shake off.

Weeds lift out most easily from soil that is damp but not sticky. Squeeze a handful of bed soil: if it crumbles, weed now; if it smears and sticks, wait a day; if it is dust or baked hard, water the evening before.

Then the stroke, with the BAGIYA 5-Teeth Weeding Rake Head:
1. Set the teeth into the soil just behind the weed.
2. Pull the head toward you.
3. Shake the soil off the roots, back onto the bed.

A pot held at arm's length loads the back far more than the same pot held close.

The hardest soil in your bed is where your foot was.

Every step inside a bed presses the soil shut. That patch drains slowly, roots stay shallow in it, and the weeds that come up there are the hardest ones to pull. The fix is in the layout, not in the digging: keep a bed narrow enough that you can reach its middle from the path, and put your feet on the path only.

Moss is not a sign of a dirty path. It is a sign of shade and damp.

Moss has no true roots. It holds on with fine threads and needs a surface that stays wet, which is why it shows up on the shaded side of a path, under a tree or along a wall, and not on the side the sun reaches. Scrubbing clears it for a while. Letting in light and giving the water somewhere to go is what keeps it away.

Four weeds in a vegetable bed. Each one comes out a different way.

Doob creeps by runners that root at every joint: find the runner and lift its whole length, because a piece left behind grows again.
Motha (nutgrass): the top snaps off and the tubers stay, so loosen the soil under it first, then lift.
Bathua has one upright stem and one straight root: it comes out whole when the soil is damp and the plant is young. Many homes cook the young leaves as saag.
Kulfa (luni) has a fleshy stem that can root again from a broken piece: carry it off the bed, do not leave it lying on damp soil.

Weeds in a gravel path do not come up from below. They land on top.

Dust, silt and leaf litter settle between the stones and slowly become a thin layer of soil. Wind-blown seeds sprout in that layer and root down through the gaps. The packed base underneath is not where they start.

That thin layer between the stones is the root zone, and it is where weed killer granules act. They clear whatever they reach, so never use them on lawns, beds or crops you are keeping. Wear gloves; keep away from children, pets and plants you want.

A spade cannot reach the foot of a wall.

Weeds along a wall root into the joint where the wall meets the ground. You cannot dig that joint out without chipping the plaster, so the top gets pulled, the root stays, and that line is the first to grow back.

BAGIYA Weed Killer Granules go there by hand. No spray, no mixing: sprinkle them at the base, water lightly, and leave it. They work at the root.

The honest part: the granules clear whatever they reach. Use them only on ground you want completely clear, such as the foot of a boundary wall, and never on lawns, beds or crops you are keeping. Wear gloves, and keep them away from children, pets and plants you want.

The weeding that matters most is the first one.

In the first few weeks after sowing, your seedlings and the weeds are the same height. They want the same light and the same water, and the weeds are usually quicker.

Once the crop's leaves close over the soil, the ground underneath is shaded and far fewer weeds come up. So the early pass, while the weeds are still small and come out easily, does more for the bed than any later one.

What you see is the smaller half of a weed.

In grasses and weeds that come back season after season, much of the plant lives below the surface: roots, runners, tubers. That is why cutting the top only buys a few weeks.

Weed killer granules go onto the soil at the base and are watered in lightly, so they work at the root. No spray, no mixing: sprinkle, water lightly, leave it. They clear whatever they reach, so never use them on lawns, beds or crops you are keeping. Wear gloves; keep away from children, pets and plants you want.

Most of the grass in your bed walked in from the edge.

Creeping grasses like doob send runners sideways from a lawn or a path into a bed. A bed with a soft, grassy edge is refilled from that side all season. Cut a clean edge, keep a narrow strip bare between the grass and the bed, and make a pass along it every time you weed: the runners show up in the strip first, where they are easy to lift.

Clear a weed before it flowers, not after.

A weed that has flowered has already set seed. Clearing it then removes this plant but leaves next season's crop of weeds in the soil. The time to act is when you see buds, so walk your plot and look for them now.

Three weeds you can tell apart with your fingers.

Nutgrass (கோரை · తుంగ గడ్డి · മുത്തങ്ങ): roll the stem between finger and thumb. It is triangular, with sharp edges, and the glossy leaves come out in threes. Sedges have edges.
Doob grass (அருகம்புல் · గరిక · കറുക): flat, wiry stems that creep along the ground and put down roots at every joint.
Congress grass (பார்த்தீனியம் · వయ్యారిభామ · പാർത്തീനിയം): finely cut, carrot-like leaves and tiny white flower heads. Pull it with gloves on.

Why the name matters: nutgrass and doob come back from what is below the ground, so the root has to go. Congress grass comes back from its seed, so it has to be cleared before it flowers.

You are watering your weeds too.

Weed seeds wait in the top layer of every bed, and they sprout wherever that layer gets wet. A pipe that soaks the whole bed wakes all of them, in every gap between your rows. Water given only at each plant's base wets the soil where its roots feed and leaves the gaps dry, so far fewer weeds come up there.
